title: Windowsill or Patio Colour Census
introduction: A gentle start: stay in your own garden or balcony and count the colours hiding in plain sight. No walking far, no gear, just your eyes.
steps: Stand somewhere in your garden or on your balcony and take three slow breaths.
Scan slowly from left to right and silently count every distinct colour you can find: greens, browns, flower tones, pot colours, even rust or paint.
Pick the three rarest colours and notice where each one sits in the space.
Crouch down and look again from knee height, then stand up and finish with one last slow scan to see if the count changed.
observation_goal: Find at least six distinct colours in your garden or balcony space, including two shades of green.
completion_condition: You can name your six colours and the rarest one you spotted before heading back inside.
safety_notes: Stay on paths and paved areas; step over garden tools and hoses rather than on them.
Keep traffic in mind if your garden borders a road: stay back from the edge and keep an eye on cars.
Do not taste or touch unknown plants, berries, or insects while observing them.

title: Park Bench Sound Map
introduction: Find a bench or a patch of grass in your local park and map the invisible world of sound around you for a few quiet minutes.
steps: Choose a safe spot away from paths and sit or stand comfortably.
Close your eyes for one minute and count how many separate sound sources you can name.
Open your eyes and for each sound, guess its direction and distance: near, middle, far.
Look for one sound you cannot identify, then take one more minute to notice the quietest layer of sound underneath the rest.
observation_goal: Identify at least four distinct sound sources and their rough directions.
completion_condition: You have noted four sounds with directions and picked out the quiet background layer.
safety_notes: Stay on open lawn or paved areas and keep aware of cyclists, runners, and traffic near park edges.
Keep to well-used parts of the park and follow any road or path signage.
Observe birds and other wildlife from a distance; never feed or chase them.

title: Front-Step Nature Window
introduction: Step just outside your front door and treat the first ten meters of your neighborhood as a tiny nature reserve to observe.
steps: Stand on your step or by your gate and look up at the sky for thirty seconds.
Find three living things: a plant, an insect, or a bird, all viewed from a safe distance.
Notice one sign of the season: a changing leaf, a bud, a cobweb, or bare branches.
Look at one building or wall closely, then watch one bird or one swaying branch for a full minute without moving.
observation_goal: Spot three living things and one clear sign of the current season.
completion_condition: You can name your three living things and the seasonal sign before going back inside.
safety_notes: Stay on the pavement or your own property; never step into the road or a driveway to look closer.
Be traffic-aware at all times: cars may pull out of driveways, so keep to safe ground.
Look but do not touch unknown plants or insects, and wash your hands after being outdoors.

title: Balcony or Garden Breath-and-Leaf Loop
introduction: A slightly longer stay in your own green space, pairing slow breathing with close observation of a single plant.
steps: Water your plant beds if they need it, or simply dampen your hands and notice the smell of soil.
Choose one plant and study a single leaf: outline, veins, edges, and any bite marks from insects.
Trace the leaf's shape with your eyes (not your fingers) and count the main veins.
Look up and find two plants or trees that share a similar leaf shape.
Sit quietly for two minutes and watch how the chosen leaf moves in the breeze.
Close by naming three things you saw today that you had never noticed before.
observation_goal: Describe one leaf in detail and find two other plants with a similar leaf shape.
completion_condition: You have studied one leaf closely and matched it against two other plants in the space.
safety_notes: Stay on paths and stable ground; watch your footing on wet tiles or soil.
If your garden borders a road, keep traffic in mind and stay a step back from the edge.
Observe insects from a distance and never handle unknown insects or taste any plant part.

title: Five-Tree Personality Portraits
introduction: Take a slow loop through your nearest park and give five trees a personality based only on what you can observe.
steps: Walk a easy loop and stop at the first tree that catches your eye.
Study its trunk texture, branch angles, and height, then invent a one-word personality for it.
Repeat for a second tree and notice how different its bark and shape are.
Find a third tree with leaves still on it and compare leaf shapes with the first two.
Sit for a few minutes near your favourite of the five and watch its movement in the wind.
On the way back, pick the tree you would like to visit again and say why out loud.
observation_goal: Observe five trees closely enough to describe their bark, shape, and one distinguishing feature each.
completion_condition: You have five one-word tree personalities and a favourite you can justify.
safety_notes: Keep to established park paths and stay clear of any road around the park boundary.
Watch for cyclists and other people on shared paths; step aside politely.
Do not climb trees or fences, and give nests and wildlife a wide berth.

title: Street-Level Texture Hunt
introduction: A slower neighborhood walk with a mission: collect visual textures instead of objects, and notice how built and living things mix.
steps: Plan a short loop entirely on pavements and crossings, then set off at an unhurried pace.
Spot and photograph or mentally note five textures: brick, bark, leaf, metal, fabric-like moss or lichen.
For each texture, guess what made it: weather, growth, people, or time.
Find one place where a plant is quietly reclaiming a wall, crack, or fence.
Stop at a safe crossing and watch how wind moves through one tree or hedge for a minute.
Finish by choosing the texture you would most like to touch with clean hands later, and why.
observation_goal: Collect five different textures and identify one plant reclaiming a built surface.
completion_condition: All five textures noted, one reclamation spot found, and the wind-watching minute completed.
safety_notes: Cross only at crossings or quiet junctions and stay on the pavement at all times.
Traffic comes first: stop looking at textures whenever you are near or crossing a road.
Do not touch unknown plants, fungi, or insects; observe them from a short distance.

title: Slow Park Audit Walk
introduction: Thirty minutes of deliberate wandering with a purpose: notice what makes this park feel alive, and what would make it better.
steps: Walk a slow full loop of the park and notice light, shade, and open space.
Stop three times for two minutes each: once to listen, once to watch movement, once to smell the air.
Find evidence of wildlife you cannot see: feathers, nibbled leaves, holes, or tracks.
Pick one spot you would return to with a book and describe what makes it work.
Notice one maintenance or safety issue, such as broken lighting, without touching or entering anything.
Close your loop with a two-minute standstill observation of one wide view.
Recall your three favourite micro-moments on the walk home in your head.
observation_goal: Collect three two-minute observations plus one piece of wildlife evidence.
completion_condition: You completed the full loop, the three timed stops, and identified a favourite reading spot.
safety_notes: Keep to lit, well-used paths and stay aware of roads and traffic at every park boundary.
Follow park signage and stay out of any closed, fenced, or restricted sections.
Observe wildlife evidence from a distance; do not touch feathers, nests, or animal traces.

title: Evening Block Sensory Circuit
introduction: A half-hour circuit around your own block using one sense at a time, ideal for winding down before the day ends.
steps: Check the light and weather, wear something visible, and plan a loop on quiet pavements.
First block segment: hearing only. Note every sound and its direction.
Second segment: sight only. Count birds, moving branches, and lit windows.
Third segment: smell only. Name three scents: soil, food, plants, rain, or city air.
Pause at a safe spot for a two-minute standstill and notice how your breathing settles.
Finish the loop and recap one highlight for each sense before heading home.
observation_goal: Complete one observation for each of hearing, sight, and smell while walking the loop.
completion_condition: Full loop finished with one highlight recorded per sense and the standstill pause done.
safety_notes: Wear something visible, carry a light if it is dark, and stay on pavements away from traffic.
Cross at crossings only and keep awareness on roads even while focused on a single sense.
Leave unknown plants and animals alone; report any unleashed or stray animals from a distance.

title: Rooftop, Courtyard, or Veranda Sky Log
introduction: For any safe shared outdoor space: a half-hour sky-watching session that needs nothing but a chair and your attention.
steps: Set up in a safe, open spot with a clear view of the sky and secure railings behind you.
Watch for five minutes and log every cloud type you can distinguish.
Track one bird or aircraft across the sky and note its direction and speed compared to others.
Watch how the light changes on one building or plant over five minutes.
Listen for five minutes and note which sounds arrive from above versus around you.
Close with a two-minute pause, then write or say three things the sky taught you today.
observation_goal: Log at least two cloud types, one tracked moving object, and one light change.
completion_condition: The cloud log, the tracked object, the light change, and the closing pause are all done.
safety_notes: Stay behind railings or on stable, level ground and keep away from edges at all times.
If the space borders a road, keep traffic in mind and never lean over to look down.
Do not use binoculars or screens continuously; keep eyes on your footing when moving.
